points.title: Number base
points.must: The base is the number of different digits a system uses and the multiplier between place values; denary base 10, binary base 2, hexadecimal base 16.

points.title: Binary, denary and hexadecimal compared
points.must: Digits of each system (0–1; 0–9; 0–9 and A–F with A=10 … F=15) and their place values (1, 2, 4 … 128; 1, 10, 100; 1, 16, 256).

points.title: Who uses each system
points.must: Hardware uses binary; people use denary; programmers use hexadecimal as a short form of binary.

points.title: Why computers use binary
points.must: Transistors / circuits have two states (on/off, high/low voltage) that represent 1 and 0; two states are reliable and easy to tell apart.

points.title: Bit, nibble, byte
points.must: Bit = one binary digit; nibble = 4 bits (one hex digit); byte = 8 bits (0–255).

points.title: Number of values in n bits
points.must: n bits store 2ⁿ values; the largest is 2ⁿ − 1 (8 bits: 256 values, largest 255); one more bit doubles the range.

points.title: Powers of 2 table
points.must: A table of 2ⁿ and 2ⁿ − 1 for n = 1 to 8 (and 16).

points.title: Minimum number of bits
points.must: A worked example such as 150 lockers need 8 bits because 7 bits only give 128 numbers.

points.title: Binary → denary
points.must: Write place values 128 … 1 above the bits and add those with a 1, with an example (e.g. 10110110 = 182).

points.title: Quick checks
points.must: Ends in 1 → odd; leftmost bit of 8 is worth 128; leading zeros do not change the value.

points.title: Denary → binary: place-value method
points.must: Subtract the largest place value that fits, write 1 or 0 for each place, with an example (156 = 10011100) and a check.

points.title: Denary → binary: division method
points.must: Divide by 2 repeatedly, note remainders, read them from the bottom up (e.g. 47 = 101111 = 00101111).

points.title: Common mistakes
points.must: Remainders read top-down; rightmost bit is worth 1; give 8 bits when asked; 256 values but largest 255.
